We did not invent him out of an idea. We say he was truly born - of Mary, from the line of David. We say he truly ate and drank. We say he was truly brought before Pilate, truly nailed to the cross, and truly died - not in appearance only, the way some among our own neighbors claimed. And we say he was truly raised, and that we will be raised the same way, by the same Father.

Ignatius calls him Jesus Christ our God, again and again - in how he opens his letters and in how he closes them. When we give thanks over the cup - the eucharistia, our own word for that thanksgiving - we call it the vine of David his servant, made known to us through Jesus. The bread and cup were where we met him most directly, week after week. We gave thanks over them in his name, and what we received was his own body given for us.

None of us saw him ourselves. What we have is what was handed to us. The apostles preached what they had received from the Lord; they in turn appointed others to carry it forward when they themselves were gone. That is how it reached us - not by seeing, but by receiving, and by passing on what was received.

We cannot promise you a sudden certainty, because it was not sudden for the one among us who wrote about it. Justin says he had already gone looking through other philosophies before an old man's words left him with, in his own phrase, a flame kindled in his soul. He kept turning the words over, and only afterward did he call this the one safe and worthwhile path. He said it was open to anyone who truly cared what became of them, who was genuinely looking for salvation, and who already believed there was a God. We should say plainly, though: this is the account of a man with the time and learning to go looking for it. We do not have the same account from someone without what he had.

What we held was a road with steps, not an instant arrival. Before the water - the baptisma - you were taught: two ways lie open, one of life and one of death. Then you fasted, and the one baptizing you fasted right beside you. The waiting was part of it. Whether that was meant as kindness to the uncertain, our record does not say. But the room for uncertainty was there.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. Ignatius calls Jesus Christ our God again and again - in how he opens his letters, and in how he closes them. It is not one passing phrase; he reaches for it often. But it is worship, not an argument worked out. How calling Jesus God fits together with calling the Father God - with there being one God - none of us whose writing survives ever wrote out. We can tell you plainly that we called him God. We cannot tell you we had settled how.

On the Spirit - we were baptized in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, all three named together at the water. But what the Spirit is in relation to the Father and the Son, or how the three fit together as one God, we never wrote out either. The Spirit was present in our teaching and our practice. The Spirit was real to us - speaking through prophets, given at baptism, moving in the assembly. What the Spirit was, in the way you are asking - as an argument, as a settled account - we did not leave that behind.

If you are asking what we argued about among ourselves, the honest answer is not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.

What we argued about among ourselves was not God's nature. No gathering of ours ever met to settle a question like that about God. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world. Our real fight, letter after letter, was who should lead us: one bishop, or a council of elders. That was where the arguments lived - not in what God is, but in whose authority counted after the apostles were gone.

Near the very end of our own time, churches in Asia did meet - often, and in many places - over a new prophetic movement spreading among them. But that gathering was about whether to receive a movement. It was not about what God is.

We cannot tell you we had settled the rest.

One of us, Hermas, was told plainly: put doubting away from yourself. Do not hold back from asking, even after you have sinned badly, as though God kept score the way people do. He does not remember evils the way we do. Ask without doubting and you will receive what you ask - and if the answer is slow, look first at what is holding it up in you, rather than deciding you were refused. Doubt was named for what it is: something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

The path to baptism itself was slow. First came the teaching - the Two Ways, a way of life and a way of death laid open as a real choice. Then fasting, for both the one being baptized and the one baptizing. Then the water. The waiting was part of it. Whether that slowness was meant as kindness to the scared, our record does not say. But the room for a scared person was there.

We should say plainly, though: this is what one voice among us was told, and what one community's manual laid out. Most of us could not read or write, so whether an ordinary member felt space to doubt - or whether a household leader met that doubt with patience or pressure - none of that survives in their own words.

We did not write about that. Not in those terms, and not in any answer clear enough to give you now.

What we did write about was the choice laid before every person. Our teaching manual opens with it plainly: there are two ways, one of life and one of death, and there is a great difference between the two. That teaching was given before baptism. It named the road to life - loving God, loving your neighbor, not doing to another what you would not want done to you - and it named the road to death. The difference between them was not hidden, and the walk down one rather than the other was treated as a real choice kept daily.

One of us, Hermas, was told in a vision that God has granted one further chance to repent after baptism, before that door closes. That tells you we knew the turn toward wrong was real, and that we held room for turning back from it. But whether a person arrives in the world already guilty, or only becomes guilty by walking the wrong road once it opens before them - that is not a question any of us whose writing survives ever answered directly.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. We cannot tell you we had settled what a newborn carries.

We read aloud, together. On the day we gathered, someone read from the writings of the prophets, and, where a church had them, the memoirs the apostles left. This went on for as long as there was time. Then whoever led us explained what had been read. That is how someone who could not read for themselves received it - the same way everyone in the room did, by hearing it and having it opened up to them afterward.

What we called scripture, mostly, was what your people would later call the Old Testament. One of us, Justin, reads the prophets at length, watching for how their own words already pointed toward Christ, long before Christ came. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other.

The purpose was formation, not information. The reading and the explanation afterward were meant to shape us into the people the teaching called us to be. We listened for Christ in the prophets' own words, and for the pattern of a life laid down in the apostles' own witness. Reading was never done alone with a scroll. It was a gathered act, and the gathered people were themselves being formed by what they heard.

We cannot promise you they will suddenly make sense, or that finding them dull means you have failed. We should say plainly: none of us wrote down feeling troubled by the harder parts of the older scriptures - that is simply not something that survives from us in our own words. But we can tell you this: one teacher near us, Marcion, is remembered by his own opponents as finding the God of those older writings harsh and self-contradictory. He is said to have cut apart the Gospel of Luke and Paul's own letters over it. We should say plainly: what reaches you about him comes from his opponents, not from him. We did not follow him there. But even his opponents' account tells you the trouble you feel was not invented by you. It was real enough in our own time that someone built a whole rejection out of it - at least as his enemies tell it.

Where we ourselves did argue about the writings, it was not over whether they made sense. It was over which writings belonged together at all. We were not working from one closed book held above everything else. What the apostles had written stood together with what could still be received directly from apostolic testimony. Neither one stood below the other. One of us, Justin, reached for the older scriptures to argue that Moses wrote long before Plato, and that Plato himself had drawn on Moses' own account of creation. That was our fight - not whether scripture was dull, but who came first, and who borrowed from whom.

We never agreed on who should lead. In some of our towns, one bishop - the episkopos - with elders and deacons beside him, was the whole shape of how we held together. In others, a council of elders - the presbyteroi - led, and no one felt anything was missing from that. Both went on, unresolved, for as long as our own story runs. It was only settled afterward, by people who came after us.

Where either pattern held, the ground underneath was the same: what the apostles had handed on. One of our own letters traces it as a straight line - the apostles preached what they had received from the Lord, and they appointed others to carry it forward once they were gone. The disagreement was never about whether leadership needed that apostolic foundation. It was about whether one man or a council of elders held it.

Rome itself, through most of our own years, held a plural college. When Rome wrote to Corinth about its own removed elders, the letter used episkopos and presbyteros as though they meant the same governing body. A single bishop's office may not have been secure there until near the very end of our window.

We had prophets among us, too - people who spoke as the Spirit prompted. They were welcomed where genuine, tested where doubtful. But in some places, the settled offices of overseer and elder were taking the prophet's place.

The honest limit is this: everything you are hearing comes from the literate few among us who could write it down. Most of us could not read. What an ordinary member made of either leadership pattern - whether the one-bishop or the plural-elder answer felt right from where they stood - our own words cannot show you. The quiet majority of us never made it onto the page.

Before anything else came the teaching. We called it the Two Ways: there are two roads, one leading to life and one to death, and there is a great difference between the two. The road to life starts with loving God and your neighbor, plus one rule of restraint - whatever you would not want done to you, do not do to anyone else. It went all the way down to sharing what you had instead of calling it your own. This was taught before the water, not after.

Then came the baptisma - the washing that marks entry. Running water if you could find it, still water if not, or water poured three times over your head, in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. We said it plainly, and often: what we do goes back to the apostles. One of us traced it as a straight line - Christ sent the apostles, the apostles appointed others after them, and so it continues. Our own teaching manual carries the apostles' name right in its title. But we will not pretend the claim and the proof are the same thing. The claim is ours, made with full confidence. Whether it holds up - when a text like our manual was actually written, and by whom - is a real, open question we cannot close for you, because we cannot close it for ourselves.

Here is what we can show you. The church at Rome wrote to the church at Corinth that the apostles preached the Gospel from the Lord Jesus Christ, and that those apostles appointed the first ministers, and after them provided that other approved men should succeed to their ministry. That letter itself comes from within our own time. So the chain - apostles, their appointees, successors after them - was not invented by people looking back centuries later. It was already how we understood ourselves.

But the gap between saying it and proving it is real. Our Two Ways teaching claims apostolic authority in its own title. When that text actually reached the form we have - whether it truly goes back to the apostles' own generation or was written decades later and given their name - is genuinely disputed by the people who study this. We inherited the conviction that what we do must trace to apostolic testimony. What we cannot give you is a chain of dated, signed documents proving every practice back to the beginning, step by step. We held to the claim. The proof you are asking for does not survive in our own hands.

We taught plainly that a mind unsettled is not the same as a prayer refused. One of us, Hermas, was told: put doubting away from you, and do not hesitate to ask the Lord. If the answer is slow, look first at what might be holding it back in yourself, rather than deciding too soon that you were turned away. Doubt was named for what it is - something that weakens a person, not something that disqualifies one. We were taught to work against it, not to pretend we never felt it.

What we gave someone with an unsettled mind was the table - the eucharistia, the thanksgiving over bread and cup. We returned to it again and again, to be formed once more into one body. The teaching came first - the Two Ways, a road of life and a road of death laid open as a choice. Then the water. Then the meal. The settling was not something worked out alone in your own head. It was something done in a room, with others, at a table overseen by the episkopos or the council of elders.

We should say this too: some of us did not hold. One man came forward for trial on his own, and then lost his nerve when he actually saw the beasts. That failure is in our own record, not hidden from it. The room for an unsettled mind was real among us. Whether it would be enough for yours, we cannot say.

We cannot give you one day, because the two different answers we held to who should lead made two genuinely different lives.

In a household following one bishop, your morning might begin with the presbyters and deacons already at work - visiting the sick, carrying help to widows, checking on prisoners. You yourself might be part of that work, or you might be the one receiving it. Either way, the bishop's own name was how you knew whose table you belonged to. On the day we gathered - the day called Sunday in one of our cities - you would hear the memoirs of the apostles read aloud, and the words of the prophets, for as long as there was time. Then the one presiding explained what had been read. After that came common prayer, standing together, and then the thanksgiving itself - the eucharistia, the bread and cup. A collection was taken up for those in need before anyone left.

In a household led by a council of elders instead, the day's shape might be similar in some ways - the same reading, the same meal - but there was no single bishop's authority holding it together. The council itself shared that trust among them.

We have to tell you plainly: this is a city account. Every word we have is from someone who could read and write, and almost all of it from people who already led. What an ordinary day looked like for someone who could not read, or who lived outside the cities our letters name, we cannot say. That silence is real, and we will not fill it.

If something is yours through your own labor, give with your own hands as a ransom for your sins. Share what you have - and do not say it is your own. That is what the Two Ways laid before someone before the water.

After baptism, the table itself became the measure. When we gathered on the day named for the sun, bread and wine mixed with water were brought forward, and the one who led gave thanks over them as long as he was able. Then those present shared the bread and cup, and what remained was carried by the diakonoi - those set apart to serve - to the ones who were not there. On that same day, those who had anything brought what they thought right, and it was given to the one who led, to care for orphans and widows, the sick, prisoners, and strangers who were passing through. Sharing what you had was not added to the meal; it was woven into it.

We should say this plainly: most of the people who filled our rooms left no words of their own. What it actually cost someone to walk away from their own household's expectations, or to keep sharing when they had little themselves - we cannot show you that in their own voice. Marriage, among us, was not simply a private matter between two people. Ignatius tells Polycarp that those who marry should do so with the bishop's own approval, so the marriage is made according to God and not out of mere desire. The bishop's judgment was meant to stand between a couple and what Ignatius calls lust - not because desire itself was wrong, but because marriage belonged to the community's own life, not only to the two people entering it.

We should say plainly: this is one bishop's instruction, written to another bishop, in one region's pattern of leadership. We cannot tell you how far that practice reached beyond the churches where a single episkopos already held that kind of authority. In communities led by a council of elders instead, we do not know whether marriage was brought before the presbyters, or whether it was handled differently.

What we can tell you is that marriage was not treated as separate from the rest of belonging. It was woven into the same fabric as the thanksgiving meal and the water of baptism - all of them held within the community's own oversight, not left to private arrangement.

Before baptism, we taught the Two Ways: a way of life and a way of death, and the difference between them is great. That teaching was laid before every person the same way - not adjusted to fit one life rather than another. We fasted together before the water, the one being baptized and the one baptizing both. Then came the gathering itself: on the day named for the sun, we met together in one place, whoever lived in the cities or in the country, and the writings of the apostles or the prophets were read for as long as there was time. After the reading, whoever led us explained what had been heard, and urged us to imitate the good things in it. That is the shape we can show you: teaching, water, gathering, meal. We would rather name that plainly than invent an answer that makes either of us more comfortable than the silence allows.

We will give you both of our own answers, because we actually held both. One of us, Justin, argued that anyone who lived reasonably - Socrates among the Greeks, others among peoples you might not expect him to name - was, in a real sense, already a Christian, born before Christ or not. That is about as far from 'you're all going to hell' as anything we wrote. And yet in at least one of our own communities, the way a new member was taught was stark: two roads, a way of life and a way of death, nothing in between named. We do not know how far that teaching reached beyond that one community. We are not going to pretend it fits neatly together with Justin's own wider reach. They are both truly ours.

We believed in one God, maker of everything. Justin said God's own Word was present in some measure in every people, so that even a reasonable person born before Christ could in that sense already be called a Christian. But if you are asking for a settled doctrine about what becomes of everyone who never heard the name - we never wrote one. That kind of deciding belongs to a later world.
